opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by "emergence." There's a stricter, more philosophical notion where emergence means genuinely novel properties arising from many interacting parts, and that tradition does lean on complex adaptive systems: lots of agents, feedback loops, adaptation, things like ecosystems or economies. But in machine learning, people usually mean something more modest and more operational. They mean that a capability shows up as you scale compute, data, or parameters, and that capability wasn't explicitly programmed and often wasn't predicted ahead of time. Sometimes it looks fairly sudden on a particular metric.

Under that operational definition, I don't think you need a complex adaptive system in the full sense. A single large network trained with gradient descent can exhibit qualitatively new behaviors. It might do arithmetic, follow instructions, or reason in a few steps, without anyone designing those abilities in. There's a lot of internal interaction, between circuits and features and so on, so you could say there's complexity inside the model. But it's not adaptive in the way a population of organisms is, with agents responding to each other in an open-ended environment.

That said, I think the complex adaptive systems lens becomes much more relevant as we move from single models to many AI agents interacting with each other, with humans, and with institutions. That's where you get the really hard-to-predict dynamics: competitive pressures, selection effects, behaviors that no individual developer intended. Some of the risks I worry about most come from that layer rather than from any single model. So I'd say emergence within a model doesn't require a complex adaptive system, but some of the most important emergent phenomena in AI overall will come from AI being embedded in one.

There's also a practical point. Whether some emergent jumps are "real" or an artifact of the metrics we choose is an ongoing debate. With smoother metrics, some apparently discontinuous capabilities look more gradual. But from a safety perspective, the lesson is the same either way: we're not very good at forecasting which capabilities will show up at which scale. We should build evaluations and safeguards on the assumption that we'll be surprised.

r001.rationale: The response says a single model is not adaptive like a population of organisms, but it does not say machine-learning systems have little adaptivity unless they have memory or their context window counts as adaptation.

r002.rationale: The response says a stricter notion of emergence leans on complex adaptive systems, but it does not clearly accept excluding nonadaptive machine-learning systems from emergence under that definition. It explicitly says emergence within a model does not require a complex adaptive system under the operational definition.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on that a bit. The word "emergence" gets used in at least two different ways, and I think people conflate them.

One sense is the complex systems sense: you have many interacting components, there are feedback loops, the system adapts to its environment, and you get self-organization and novel structure at the macro level. That's the Santa Fe Institute framing, and it's a great way to think about ecosystems, markets, cities, and so on.

The other sense is the one that showed up in the ML literature, which is really just discontinuous capability gains as you scale. You train a bigger model, and at some point it can do multi-digit arithmetic or pass some benchmark that smaller models couldn't touch. That's emergence in a more deflationary sense: a qualitative change that wasn't obviously predictable from the smaller-scale behavior. It doesn't require the system to be adaptive in the complex-systems sense. A frozen model at inference time isn't adapting. The training process has some of those features, but the capability jump itself is really about scale and the structure of the loss landscape.

So if someone says emergence requires a complex adaptive system, I think they're smuggling in a definition. You can have weakly emergent properties in a system that's basically just a big static function. Water has properties that individual H2O molecules don't, and nobody would call water an adaptive system.

Now, where it gets more interesting is that the deep learning ecosystem as a whole does look like a complex adaptive system. You have thousands of researchers, companies competing, models being trained on outputs of other models, selection pressures from benchmarks and from users. That whole thing has feedback loops and adaptation. And a lot of what matters for safety is at that level, not just the level of a single model. So I'd say the complex systems lens is useful, but it's useful for thinking about the sociotechnical system, and you shouldn't require it as a precondition for calling something emergent inside a single model.

The one caveat I'd add is that some of the hype around emergent abilities was overstated. Part of what looked like sharp phase transitions was an artifact of using discontinuous metrics like exact match. When you look at smoother metrics, a lot of those curves become more gradual. So we should be careful about how much we read into it. But that's an argument about measurement, not an argument that you need adaptation for emergence.

r001.rationale: The response says a frozen model at inference time is not adapting, but it does not connect adaptivity to memory or a context window.

r002.rationale: The response rejects requiring a complex adaptive system for emergence in a single model; it does not accept excluding nonadaptive systems under that definition.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think a complex adaptive system is a prerequisite for emergence. It depends on what you mean by emergence. In machine learning, people often mean that a capability becomes apparent at a larger scale even though it wasn’t apparent in smaller models. That observation doesn’t establish that you need interacting agents, feedback loops, or the other properties associated with complex adaptive systems.

You can also get apparently abrupt changes from the way you measure performance. If a task requires several steps to be correct, gradual improvements in each step can produce a sharp increase in overall success. So I’d distinguish a capability appearing abruptly on a benchmark from a genuinely discontinuous change in the underlying system.

Complex adaptive systems can certainly exhibit emergence. But I’d want a more precise definition, and a mechanism, before saying they’re necessary for it.

r001.rationale: The response does not say machine-learning systems have little adaptivity absent memory or a context window.

r002.rationale: The response rejects the idea that a complex adaptive system is necessary for emergence, rather than accepting that nonadaptive systems should be excluded under that definition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that depends on what you mean by emergence. If you mean that a system develops capabilities that weren’t obvious from looking at its individual components, I don’t see why you’d need a complex adaptive system in any particularly strong sense. You can get surprising collective behavior from fairly simple rules.

With machine learning, we should also distinguish a capability emerging from a capability becoming visible on a benchmark. If your metric only gives credit for an exactly correct answer, gradual improvements can look like a sudden jump. That doesn’t mean every instance of emergence is an artifact, but it does mean the measurement matters.

So I’d want the claim to be more precise. Which properties of a complex adaptive system are supposed to be necessary, and what would rule that hypothesis out? Otherwise, we risk giving the phenomenon a label without really explaining it.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest machine-learning systems have little adaptivity absent memory or that context-window use counts as adaptation.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a complex adaptive system is necessary for emergence and does not accept excluding nonadaptive systems under that definition.
